messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maya was 20, a young auditor from a Pacific Islander family, single, and only a year into her first full-time job when the stalking began to reshape ordinary life. At first it was just a man lingering outside her apartment after dusk, the same dark car slowly circling her building, anonymous messages that somehow seemed to know when she had left work late. By the time she reported it, she had already started checking the locks three and four times, scanning reflections in shop windows, and taking the long route home so she would not be predictable. The fear was not only of being seen, but of being known too well. What made it worse was that the stalking invaded the places that were supposed to feel routine and safe: the walk from the train to her office, the lobby of her apartment, even the quiet moments when she was trying to concentrate on spreadsheets at her desk. She began to feel that the world itself had become dangerous, and that she had to be on guard all the time, because danger could appear anywhere and from anyone.

After the first months, Maya’s thinking hardened around the idea that her life had been destroyed by what happened. She spoke about the future as if it had been taken from her, not postponed. Before the stalking, she had imagined moving out with friends, saving for travel, and building a steady career; now even making plans for the weekend felt like tempting fate. She stopped looking forward to things that might have made her feel happy or hopeful, because any moment of ease seemed fragile and almost irresponsible. If she let herself enjoy a dinner with coworkers or say yes to a spontaneous beach trip, she would later feel exposed, as if she had been careless. Her apartment, once a place of independence, became a place she associated with scanning curtains and listening for footsteps in the hall. At work, she kept her head down, double-checked her schedule, and arranged her day so she could leave while it was still light. Going out for coffee, meeting friends, even walking to the corner shop became something she avoided whenever possible, because stepping outside meant reentering the same world she had come to believe could turn threatening without warning.

Over time, those beliefs began to turn inward. Maya had come to tell herself that she deserved to suffer because of what happened, as though the fear and the shrinking of her life were a fitting sentence. The thought was not abstract; it shaped the choices she made every day. When colleagues invited her to after-work drinks, she declined and then sat alone at home, telling herself she should not be allowed to have fun while still feeling so unsafe. When her sister urged her to go for a run or to join a community event on weekends, Maya refused, not only because she feared being followed, but because relief itself started to feel undeserved. She punished herself by avoiding anything that might feel comforting, exciting, or alive. The more she believed her life had been ruined and that the world was dangerous, the more she treated happiness like a privilege she no longer had the right to claim. The consequence was a narrowing of her days: work, home, vigilance, and the private rule that if she stayed small enough, nothing worse would happen.

By the time she sought help, Maya was exhausted by the constant vigilance and by how little of her life she recognized anymore. She came in after a recent evening at the office when she had seen a car idling near the entrance and felt herself freeze, unable to shake the conviction that she was still being watched. What frightened her most was not only the possibility that the stalking might return in the same form, but that she might never reclaim the part of herself that used to feel hopeful, open, and safe in ordinary life.
